To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

radon-related lung-cancer mortality among uranium miners in the German Democratic Republic was 2.1% per WLM (95% CI 1.8–2.4%) with a time since exposure effect and a strong inverse exposure rate effect.
radon exposure was associated with an increased risk of lung cancer among uranium miners, and the ERR/WLM was highest for young workers and for high exposures.
the radon-related ERR/WLM is 0.21 (95% CI 0.18-0.24) for this cohort of uranium miners.

the evaluation of the lung cancer risk among uranium miners of the former German mining region.
the assessment of radon-related lung carcinogenicity among uranium miners and the development of risk models.
the evaluation of the lung cancer risk of former uranium miners in Germany.

the risk is higher at high exposures and that the risk is lower at lower exposures.
the results of the present study are compatible with the results of other cohort studies, but the results do not support the notion of a linear dose-response relationship at low exposures.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
radon exposure at the levels experienced by the Wismut miners is a significant risk factor for lung cancer.
the radon-related ERR/WLM is about twice that observed in previous studies.
the risk for lung cancer in uranium miners was dependent on time after exposure, attained age and cumulative radon exposure.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ERR/WLM was not significantly different for the youngest age groups and for the oldest age groups.
the risk of lung cancer in former uranium miners is not limited to high exposures.
the risk of lung cancer in uranium miners is not only related to the total amount of exposure but is also dependent on the time since exposure.
